title: Olaudah Equiano
hookLine: kidnapped as a child, he buys his freedom, writes his story, and fights the slave trade

lines: TOWN TO TOWN WITH HIS BOOK.
cards: "Written by Himself." Three words on the title page of a book, and they're doing a lot of work.

The man who wrote them had been sold as a child, carried across the ocean in a slave ship, and given a new name by the men who owned him. He put it right on the title page: this is my story, and I wrote it.
He sold the book himself, from town to town, and spoke wherever people would listen.

teach.b: His book is called The Interesting Narrative of the Life of Olaudah Equiano, or Gustavus Vassa, the African. Both names are in the title on purpose.
Olaudah Equiano is the name he says he was born with, in an Igbo village in West Africa. Gustavus Vassa is the name an owner gave him.
In the book he tells of being kidnapped with his sister, of being torn apart from her, and of the slave ship: the crowding, the stench, the people who chose to jump into the sea rather than go on.
He was sold more than once.

Under a Quaker merchant in the Caribbean, he traded a little on the side, saved every coin, and bought his freedom. Then he came to a deep Christian faith, and the book tells that story too, full of scripture.
And here's what he did with all of it. He told it. He used scripture, the book his British readers knew, to show them what the trade was doing.
A psalm says: "Let the redeemed of the LORD say so." Say so: tell it out loud. Equiano did, plainly, as the one who had lived it, and his readers couldn't unhear it.
Some historians have asked whether he was born in Africa, or gathered his memories of it from others. Others defend his account.
Either way, his voice on the page is what readers met, and the movement against the trade used it.

how: Equiano's narrative is read in schools and churches, and many readers remember him alongside others who worked against the slave trade.

games.q: you're free now, and a Christian. you carry a story the slave traders would rather nobody heard. what do you do?
o: keep quiet and live your new life.
write your own story, put your name on it, and sell it town to town.
ask someone else to tell your story for you.
games.why: he wrote it himself, said so on the title page, and spoke wherever people would listen.

practice: Breathe out slowly, twice, and think of the voices you've heard telling their own story of slavery: Equiano today, maybe others you've read or heard; if none come to mind, that's a starting place too.
Hold this: real people wrote these accounts, and signed them with their own names. If you pray, pray for those whose stories were never written down; if you don't, just remember them.
